its arguments, so each instantiation names its own leaf — total

mentl/b0008dd:
The orchestration layer that makes incremental compilation real.
Walks an import DAG from an entry module, processes each module
exactly once in dep order, consults the .kai cache, installs
cached envs into env_handler, re-infers on miss + writes fresh cache.

Architecture:
  driver_check(entry_module) — public entry
  driver_collect_dag(entry) — depth-first post-order, returns
    [leaf_module, ..., entry_module] so deps process before importers
  driver_extract_imports(source) — lex + parse just enough to
    pull ImportStmt paths (no inference; cheap traversal)
  driver_check_module(module_name) — per-module:
    - missing source: report E_MissingModule (graceful)
    - cache_read returns Some + cache_is_hit returns true:
      install entries, skip inference (THE PERF WIN)
    - cache miss: driver_reinfer_module
  driver_reinfer_module — full lex + parse + infer; snapshot env
    before/after to extract this module's exported entries; collect
    each dep's current source hash; write fresh KaiFile
  driver_install_entries — push cached entries through env_handler

Cycles: visited set prevents infinite descent. Inka modules don't
currently form import cycles, but the discipline is forward-proof.

Env diff via snapshot: env_handler prepends entries; after infer,
the new ones are at the head of the list. driver_take_first(n)
pulls them. Simple and correct given env_handler's prepend
semantics.

Limitations honestly named:
  - Per-module overlay separation deferred to IC.3 (graph chase
    walks one global graph; module envs merge flat into env_handler)
  - Dependency-hash invalidation simplified to source-hash only;
    full chain (cache hit on M requires every dep's recorded
    imports_hashes to match dep's CURRENT hash) lives in v2 of
    driver_check_module — substrate ready, policy adjustment small
  - Diagnostics from cached modules are skipped on hit (intentional:
    if they mattered, the cache wouldn't have been written; if they
    matter NOW, the source

mentl/b00d213:
Everything in Lux is one of exactly three things:
effects (what computation does), handlers (what policy
governs effects), and Pure (the absence of effects).

The rabbit hole goes all the way down. But Pure is what
makes the rest powerful — it is the boundary that enables
memoization, parallelization, compile-time eval, and
formal verification.
